# Comparison

Even though Valibot's API resembles other solutions at first glance, the implementation and structure of the source code is very different. In the following, we would like to highlight the differences that can be beneficial for both you and your users.

## Modular design

Instead of relying on a few large functions with many methods, Valibot's API design and source code is based on many small and independent functions, each with just a single task. This modular design has several advantages.

On one hand, the functionality of Valibot can be easily extended with external code. On the other, it makes the source code more robust and secure because the functionality of the individual functions as well as special edge cases can be tested much easier through unit tests.

However, perhaps the biggest advantage is that a bundler can use the static import statements to remove any code that is not needed. Thus, only the code that is actually used ends up in the production build. This allows us to extend the functionality of the library with additional functions without increasing the bundle size for all users.

This can make a big difference, especially for client-side validation, as it reduces the bundle size and, depending on the framework, speeds up the startup time.

```ts
import * as v from 'valibot'; // 1.37 kB

const LoginSchema = v.object({
  email: v.pipe(
    v.string(),
    v.nonEmpty('Please enter your email.'),
    v.email('The email address is badly formatted.')
  ),
  password: v.pipe(
    v.string(),
    v.nonEmpty('Please enter your password.'),
    v.minLength(8, 'Your password must have 8 characters or more.')
  ),
});
```

### Comparison with Zod

For example, to validate a simple login form, [Zod](https://zod.dev/) requires [17.7 kB with esbuild](https://bundlejs.com/?q=zod&treeshake=%5B%7B+object%2Cstring+%7D%5D) and 15.18 kB with Rolldown, whereas Valibot requires only [1.37 kB](https://bundlejs.com/?q=valibot&treeshake=%5B%7B+email%2CminLength%2CnonEmpty%2Cobject%2Cstring%2Cpipe+%7D%5D). That's a 90 % reduction in bundle size. This is due to the fact that Zod's functions have several methods with additional functionalities, that cannot be easily removed by current bundlers when they are not executed in your source code.

```ts
// 17.7 kB with esbuild and 15.18 kB with Rolldown
import * as z from 'zod';

const LoginSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string()
    .min(1, 'Please enter your email.')
    .email('The email address is badly formatted.'),
  password: z.string()
    .min(1, 'Please enter your password.')
    .min(8, 'Your password must have 8 characters or more.'),
});
```

Zod v4 also introduces Zod Mini, a tree-shakable, functional variant aimed at reducing bundle size. For the same login form, Zod Mini requires approximately [6.88 kB with esbuild](https://bundlejs.com/?q=zod%2Fmini&treeshake=%5B%7B+check%2Cemail%2CminLength%2Cobject%2Cstring+%7D%5D) and 3.94 kB with Rolldown, still about 3 to 5x larger than Valibot's [1.37 kB](https://bundlejs.com/?q=valibot&treeshake=%5B%7B+email%2CminLength%2CnonEmpty%2Cobject%2Cstring%2Cpipe+%7D%5D), representing a ~73 % reduction when using Valibot over Zod Mini.

```ts
// 6.88 kB with esbuild and 3.94 kB with Rolldown
import * as z from 'zod/mini';

const LoginSchema = z.object({
  email: z.check(
    z.string(),
    z.minLength(1, 'Please enter your email.'),
    z.email('The email address is badly formatted.')
  ),
  password: z.check(
    z.string(),
    z.minLength(1, 'Please enter your password.'),
    z.minLength(8, 'Your password must have 8 characters or more.')
  ),
});
```

> Coming from [Zod](https://zod.dev/)? Read our [migration article](https://valibot.dev/blog/why-migrate-to-valibot/) to see the benefits of Valibot, and use our [migration guide](https://valibot.dev/guides/migrate-from-zod/) to migrate your schemas with confidence.

## Performance

With a schema library, a distinction must be made between startup performance and runtime performance. Startup performance describes the time required to load and initialize the library. This benchmark is mainly influenced by the bundle size and the amount of work required to create a schema. Runtime performance describes the time required to validate unknown data using a schema.

Since Valibot's implementation is optimized to minimize the bundle size and the effort of initialization, there is hardly any library that performs better in a [TTI](https://web.dev/articles/tti) benchmark. In terms of runtime performance, Valibot is in the midfield. Roughly speaking, the library is about twice as fast as [Zod](https://zod.dev/) v3, and has similar runtime performance to Zod v4 (including Zod Mini), but is much slower than [Typia](https://typia.io/) and [TypeBox](https://github.com/sinclairzx81/typebox), because we don't yet use a compiler that can generate highly optimized runtime code, and our implementation doesn't allow the use of the [`Function`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Function/Function) constructor.

> Further details on performance can be found in the [bachelor's thesis](https://valibot.dev/thesis.pdf) Valibot is based on.

In this article, I've summarized the results of comparing and verifying several trending libraries to see if Zod is truly the best fit for validation in frontend development, or if there might be other more suitable validation libraries.

If you are struggling to choose a validation library, I hope you find this helpful.

For those wondering "What is validation?", this explanation is easy to understand!

[https://wa3.i-3-i.info/word11610.html](https://wa3.i-3-i.info/word11610.html)

## **🚀 Target** Libraries

### Zod / v4

The most popular TypeScript-first schema validation library. It automatically generates types from schemas to ensure data safety.

**Features and Characteristics:**

- Intuitive syntax using method chaining (`z.string().email().min(5)`)
- Error handling without try-catch via `.safeParse()`
- Extensive schema manipulation (extension, selection, transformation, etc.)
- Type conversion features (e.g., automatic string-to-number conversion)
- Extensive ecosystem

[**Intro \| Zod** \\
\\
Introduction to Zod - TypeScript-first schema validation library with static type inference\\
\\
![zod.dev favicon image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=14&domain_url=https://zod.dev)zod.dev\\
\\
![zod.dev thumbnail image](https://embed.zenn.studio/api/optimize-og-image/37ce9145986976d60084/https%3A%2F%2Fzod.dev%2Fog.png%3Ftitle%3DIntro%26description%3DIntroduction%2520to%2520Zod%2520-%2520TypeScript-first%2520schema%2520validation%2520library%2520with%2520static%2520type%2520inference%26path%3Dzod.dev)](https://zod.dev/)

[https://zod.dev/](https://zod.dev/)

### Valibot / v1

A next-generation validation library that achieves over 90% bundle size reduction through modular design. Developed as a lightweight alternative to Zod.

**Features and Characteristics:**

- Pipeline syntax (verifies in order, e.g., string → email format with `v.pipe(v.string(), v.email())`)
- Lightweight design where only the features used are bundled
- Modular structure combining small functions
- Fast validation processing and compilation
- Optimization for mobile and Edge environments

[https://valibot.dev/](https://valibot.dev/)

### ArkType / v2

An innovative string-based validation library that is closest to TypeScript syntax. Characterized by automatic optimization through a built-in type system.

**Features and Characteristics:**

- TypeScript-like shorthand syntax (`'string>=2'` for "a string of 2 or more characters")
- Internal optimization for union type resolution
- Pre-detection of type contradictions (e.g., both number and string)
- Real-time error display in the editor
- Fast runtime validation (ideal for high-volume, high-frequency processing)

[**ArkType** \\
\\
TypeScript's 1:1 validator, optimized from editor to runtime\\
\\
![arktype.io favicon image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=14&domain_url=https://arktype.io)arktype.io\\
\\
![arktype.io thumbnail image](https://embed.zenn.studio/api/optimize-og-image/d435020223b9e0974679/https%3A%2F%2Farktype.io%2Fimage%2Fog.png)](https://arktype.io/)

[https://arktype.io/](https://arktype.io/)

## **📚 Trends and Popularity**

Here is the Star History chart (GitHub star history).

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/zenn-user-upload/e966356af177-20250928.png)

**Zod**'s momentum remains unabated, and its popularity is overwhelming compared to other validation libraries. With the significant improvement in developer experience due to the v4 upgrade, I believe its popularity will accelerate even further.

On the other hand, **Valibot** and **ArkType** are also steadily gaining popularity and have become noteworthy contenders.

Since both libraries receive continuous updates and their ecosystems are gradually becoming more active, they have the potential to become strong competitors to Zod in the future.

## 📊 Comparison and Benchmarks

I conducted a comparison and verification of each library under the following measurement conditions.

**Measurement Environment**

- Next.js 15.5.4
- Node.js v20.10.0
- TypeScript 5.x
- Measurement tool: performance.now()

**Measurement Units**

- **μs (microseconds)**: One millionth of a second (0.000001 seconds)
- **ops/s**: Operations per second
- **ms (milliseconds)**: One thousandth of a second (0.001 seconds)

### Execution Speed Comparison

**Simple Schema - Valid Data**

| Library | Average Execution Time | Processing Speed | Relative Performance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Arktype** | 0.775 μs | 1,281,600 ops/s | 1.00x (Baseline) |
| **Zod** | 0.927 μs | 1,066,714 ops/s | 1.20x slower |
| **Valibot** | 0.943 μs | 1,030,532 ops/s | 1.24x slower |

- Measured with correct data that satisfies all validation rules.

**Simple Schema - Invalid Data**

| Library | Average Execution Time | Processing Speed | Relative Performance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Arktype** | 0.518 μs | 1,930,050 ops/s | 1.00x (Baseline) |
| **Valibot** | 3.599 μs | 278,022 ops/s | 6.94x slower |
| **Zod** | 20.620 μs | 48,931 ops/s | 39.46x slower |

- Measured with invalid data that causes validation errors (e.g., insufficient characters, invalid email format).

**Complex Schema**

| Library | Average Execution Time | Processing Speed | Relative Performance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Arktype** | 0.003 ms | 378,972 ops/s | 1.00x (Baseline) |
| **Zod** | 0.059 ms | 17,271 ops/s | Approx. 21.94x slower |
| **Valibot** | 0.105 ms | 9,593 ops/s | Approx. 39.50x slower |

- Measured with large-scale data containing nested objects and arrays.

### Bundle Size Comparison

**Production Build Size (Actual Next.js values)**

| Library | Page Size | First Load JS | node\_modules | Tree-shaking Efficiency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Valibot** | 1.35 KB | 127 KB | 1.7 MB | ◎ |
| **Zod** | 1.30 KB | 171 KB | 5.6 MB | ◎ |
| **Arktype** | 1.58 KB | 162 KB | 628 KB | ⚪︎ |

**Notes**

- Valibot achieves the best tree-shaking efficiency thanks to its modular design.
- Arktype has the smallest node\_modules size, but the build size is medium because it includes a JIT compiler.
- Zod has the largest bundle size due to its rich set of features.

### Initialization Performance

| Library | Schema Creation Time | First Execution | Subsequent Executions | JIT Compilation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Valibot** | 0.014 ms | 0.119 ms | 0.012 ms | None |
| **Arktype** | 0.121 ms | 0.666 ms | 0.010 ms | Yes (66x faster) |
| **Zod** | 0.243 ms | 0.516 ms | 0.014 ms | Yes (36x faster) |

**Notes**

- Arktype is fast from the first run (JIT optimized).
- Zod has significantly improved with the introduction of JIT in v4.
- Valibot has an excellent TTI (Time to Interactive) due to its initialization-focused design.

### Other Comparison Items

| Item | Zod | Valibot | ArkType |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Execution Speed (Valid Data)** | ⚪︎ Standard | ⚪︎ Standard | ◎ Fast |
| **Execution Speed (Invalid Data)** | △ Slow | ⚪︎ Standard | ◎ Fast |
| **Execution Speed (Complex Schema)** | ⚪︎ Standard | △ Slow | ◎ Fast |
| **Bundle Size** | △ Large | ◎ Smallest | ⚪︎ Medium |
| **Next.js Integration** | ◎ Excellent | ⚪︎ Good | ⚪︎ Good |
| **Error Messages** | ◎ Detailed | ⚪︎ Good | ⚪︎ Good |
| **Custom Validation** | ◎ Flexible | ◎ Flexible | ⚪︎ Limited |
| **Asynchronous Validation** | ◎ Supported | ◎ Supported | △ Not supported (External implementation required) |
| **Server-side Usage** | ◎ Fully supported (Node.js optimized) | ◎ Fully supported (Lightweight design) | ⚪︎ Supported (Some limitations) |
| **Type Inference Performance** | ⚪︎ Standard (Heavy when complex) | ◎ Fast (Efficient) | ◎ Fastest (String parsing) |
| **Edge Runtime** | ◎ Supported (Stable operation) | ◎ Supported (Optimized) | ⚪︎ Partially supported (Verification required) |

## 🧑‍💻 Comparison of Implementation Methods

Using a "Corporate Inquiry Form" as an example, we will compare the implementation methods using each validation library.

The following five items are required as the common data structure for input data:

```
// Structure of the inquiry form used commonly across each library
interface ContactForm {
  company: string;      // Company Name (Required)
  name: string;         // Name (Required)
  email: string;        // Email Address (Required, email format)
  category: 'design' | 'engineering' | 'sales' | 'marketing';  // Category (Required, selection)
  message: string;      // Message (Required)
}
```

![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/copy-icon.svg)![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/wrap-icon.svg)

### Zod

**Schema Definition**

```
import { z } from "zod"

// Define validation rules using the method chaining approach
const contactSchema = z.object({
    company: z.string()
        .min(1, "Please enter the company name")
        .max(100, "Company name must be within 100 characters"),
    name: z.string()
        .min(1, "Please enter your name")
        .max(50, "Name must be within 50 characters"),
    email: z.string()
        .min(1, "Please enter your email address")
        .email("Please enter a valid email address"),
    category: z.enum(["design", "engineering", "sales", "marketing"], {
        message: "Please select a category",
    }),
    message: z.string()
        .min(1, "Please enter your inquiry")
        .max(1000, "Inquiry must be within 1000 characters"),
})

// Type Inference
type ContactForm = z.infer<typeof contactSchema>
```

![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/copy-icon.svg)![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/wrap-icon.svg)

**Validation Execution**

```
const handleSubmit = async (data: ContactForm) => {
    const result = contactSchema.safeParse(data)

    if (result.success) {
        // On success: result.data contains validated data
        console.log("Validated Data:", result.data)
    } else {
        // On failure: result.error.issues contains error info
        const fieldErrors: Record<string, string> = {}
        result.error.issues.forEach((issue) => {
            const fieldName = issue.path[0] as string
            if (fieldName && !fieldErrors[fieldName]) {
                fieldErrors[fieldName] = issue.message
            }
        })
        // Error display processing
    }
}
```

![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/copy-icon.svg)![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/wrap-icon.svg)

### Valibot

**Schema Definition**

```
import * as v from "valibot"

// Combine validations using the pipeline approach
const contactSchema = v.object({
    company: v.pipe(
        v.string(),
        v.minLength(1, "Please enter at least 1 character for the company name"),
        v.maxLength(100, "Company name must be within 100 characters")
    ),
    name: v.pipe(
        v.string(),
        v.minLength(1, "Please enter at least 1 character for the name"),
        v.maxLength(50, "Name must be within 50 characters")
    ),
    email: v.pipe(
        v.string(),
        v.minLength(1, "Please enter at least 1 character for the email address"),
        v.email("Please enter a valid email address")
    ),
    category: v.picklist(["design", "engineering", "sales", "marketing"]),
    message: v.pipe(
        v.string(),
        v.minLength(1, "Please enter at least 1 character for your inquiry"),
        v.maxLength(1000, "Inquiry must be within 1000 characters")
    ),
})

// Type Inference
type ContactForm = v.InferOutput<typeof contactSchema>
```

![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/copy-icon.svg)![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/wrap-icon.svg)

**Validation Execution**

```
const handleSubmit = async (data: ContactForm) => {
    // Execute validation with safeParse
    const result = v.safeParse(contactSchema, data)

    if (result.success) {
        // On success: result.output contains validated data
        console.log("Validated Data:", result.output)
    } else {
        // On failure: result.issues contains error info
        const fieldErrors: Record<string, string> = {}
        result.issues.forEach((issue) => {
            const fieldName = issue.path?.[0]?.key as string
            if (fieldName && !fieldErrors[fieldName]) {
                fieldErrors[fieldName] = issue.message
            }
        })
        // Error display processing
    }
}
```

![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/copy-icon.svg)![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/wrap-icon.svg)

### ArkType

**Schema Definition**

```
import { type } from "arktype"

// TypeScript-like type literal syntax
const contactSchema = type({
    company: "1<=string<=100",
    name: "1<=string<=50",
    email: "string",
    category: "'design'|'engineering'|'sales'|'marketing'",
    message: "1<=string<=1000"
})

// Type Inference
type ContactForm = typeof contactBaseSchema.infer

// Detailed validation implemented in a separate function
function validateContact(data: ContactForm): { valid: boolean; errors: Record<string, string> } {
    const errors: Record<string, string> = {}

    if (data.company.length === 0) {
        errors.company = "Please enter the company name"
    } else if (data.company.length > 100) {
        errors.company = "Company name must be within 100 characters"
    }

    if (data.name.length === 0) {
        errors.name = "Please enter your name"
    } else if (data.name.length > 50) {
        errors.name = "Name must be within 50 characters"
    }

    if (data.email.length === 0) {
        errors.email = "Please enter your email address"
    } else {
        const emailRegex = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/
        if (!emailRegex.test(data.email)) {
            errors.email = "Please enter a valid email address"
        }
    }

    if (data.message.length === 0) {
        errors.message = "Please enter your inquiry"
    } else if (data.message.length < 10) {
        errors.message = "Inquiry must be at least 10 characters long"
    } else if (data.message.length > 1000) {
        errors.message = "Inquiry must be within 1000 characters"
    }

    return {
        valid: Object.keys(errors).length === 0,
        errors,
    }
}
```

![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/copy-icon.svg)![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/wrap-icon.svg)

**Validation Execution**

```
const handleSubmit = async (data: ContactForm) => {
    // Step 1: Type check
    const typeCheckResult = contactBaseSchema(data)

    // Determine by checking the "problems" property
    if ("problems" in typeCheckResult) {
        // Handle type errors
        const fieldErrors: Record<string, string> = {}
        (typeCheckResult as any).problems.forEach((problem: any) => {
            const pathKey = problem.path?.[0]
            if (pathKey && !fieldErrors[pathKey]) {
                fieldErrors[pathKey] = "Input type is invalid"
            }
        })
        // Error display processing
    } else {
        // Step 2: Custom validation
        const validData = typeCheckResult as ContactForm
        const validation = validateContact(validData)

        if (validation.valid) {
            console.log("Validated Data:", validData)
        } else {
            // Handle validation errors
            setErrors(validation.errors)
        }
    }
}
```

![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/copy-icon.svg)![](https://static.zenn.studio/images/wrap-icon.svg)

### Summary

Zod and Valibot are characterized by their **intuitive and simple syntax** using method chaining or pipeline approaches. Validation rules can be understood at a glance, and since error handling is unified with `safeParse`, they offer **excellent code readability and maintainability, making them well-suited for team development**.

ArkType takes a unique approach by adopting a **TypeScript-like type literal syntax**. While basic type checks can be written concisely, implementing detailed validation or customizing error messages requires separate custom function implementations. As a result, the **amount of implementation code tends to increase, and the unique syntax may lead to a higher learning curve**.

## 📌 Personal Impressions

With the release of Zod v4, the previous issues regarding performance and bundle size have been significantly improved, and it is likely to **continue being a strong candidate for validation libraries**.

Furthermore, its ecosystem and community are overwhelmingly active compared to other libraries, and Zod seems to have the upper hand if you value maturity.

However, if you prioritize performance above all else or are building a simple application, **choosing a library specialized for specific strengths** like Valibot or ArkType might be more appropriate.

I actually tried introducing Valibot into a personal project, and I didn't encounter any particular problems or unsupported cases. I feel it is a solid candidate to consider for medium-sized applications.

## 👀 Closing

Thank you for reading to the end! ☺️

I hope this article helps you in your development, even if only a little!

I also share my learnings and insights on tech selection and in-depth analysis of the latest technologies on my personal blog. If you are interested, I would be happy if you could check it out here!

[https://techbuild.app/blog](https://techbuild.app/blog)
